notes:
Task and constraints: Construct a shortest string containing every length-n code over an alphabet of size k as a substring.
Idea: Perform recursive depth-first traversal over rolling hashes, appending a digit only when it creates an unseen length-n sequence.
Technique and why it applies: The rolling hash represents the current suffix of length n-1. Each new digit forms a candidate sequence; lookup prevents repeats, and recursion continues from the shifted hash.
Invariant: lookup contains every length-n sequence already generated, and result is the emitted prefix.
Edge cases: The initial n-1 zeros seed the first window. The recursion stops when no unused outgoing digit exists; the method relies on the de Bruijn graph traversal strategy to visit all sequences.
Complexity: It aims to visit k^n sequences, giving O(k^n) time and O(k^n) set storage, consistent with the author labels.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a bottom row can be expanded into a pyramid using the allowed adjacent-pair-to-letter transitions.
Idea: Recursively build each next row by selecting an allowed letter above each adjacent pair.
Technique and why it applies: dic maps each adjacent pair to all possible upper letters. dfs extends nxt one letter at a time; when its length is one less than arr, that row becomes the next recursive bottom.
Invariant: arr is the current row and nxt is the partially constructed row immediately above it.
Edge cases: defaultdict is referenced but not imported in the snippet. The base case checks that a two-character row has at least one allowed transition, which is sufficient to form a one-character top only after the next-row recursion is reached.
Complexity: The number of combinations can grow exponentially with row width, and recursion stores partial rows; worst-case time and space are exponential in the pyramid size. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Check whether allowed triples can build a pyramid whose bottom row is given.
Idea: Build a fixed 7-by-7 transition table, then recursively enumerate each possible next row and memoize bottom rows already proven impossible.
Technique and why it applies: For each adjacent pair, edges lists allowed upper letters. dfs fills new_bottom left to right; after a complete row is built, the helper tries to build the next level.
Invariant: lookup stores bottom strings already explored without success, preventing repeated failed searches.
Edge cases: A one-character bottom is a completed pyramid. The table size seven assumes the alphabet is A through G. A bottom pair with no allowed upper letter fails immediately.
Complexity: Search is exponential in row width and branching choices; lookup can store many distinct row strings. The author space label describes the full number of possible rows for alphabet size a and height b.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum-size set of integers such that every interval contains at least two selected integers.
Idea: Sort intervals by end ascending and start descending, then greedily add the rightmost points needed to satisfy each interval.
Technique and why it applies: Earlier-ending intervals are handled first. If the current interval lacks two points from the selected suffix, the code appends its right endpoint or the last two integers, favoring points that can also satisfy later intervals.
Invariant: ans is intended to be a sorted set of selected points satisfying all previously processed intervals.
Edge cases: The code accesses ans[-2] only when ans is truthy, but a one-element ans still makes ans[-2] fail; the condition should check length at least two. This is a correctness issue in the shown implementation.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), and the greedy pass is O(n) with O(n) output space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Minimize the size of an integer set whose intersection with every interval has at least two elements.
Idea: Sort intervals by start ascending and end descending, then process them from the right while tracking how many points each interval still needs.
Technique and why it applies: The algorithm pops intervals in reverse order and chooses consecutive values starting at the current start, decrementing need counts for earlier intervals containing each chosen value.
Invariant: cnts[i] records how many additional selected values interval i needs, while result counts selected points.
Edge cases: The method mutates intervals by sorting and popping. Its inner condition checks s <= intervals[i][1] but does not check s >= intervals[i][0], so it can decrement counts for intervals that do not contain s; correctness is questionable.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), but nested scans and repeated list pops can take O(n²) time. Storage is O(n), so the author O(n log n) time label understates this implementation.

Task and constraints: Rearrange a special binary string into the lexicographically largest possible special string.
Idea: Split the string into balanced primitive special substrings, recursively maximize their interiors, then sort the pieces descending.
Technique and why it applies: A special substring has equal counts of ones and zeros and every prefix has at least as many ones as zeros. Each time balance returns to zero, the code extracts a primitive block wrapped as 1 + interior + 0.
Invariant: balance tracks the current prefix's excess ones, and sublist contains completed primitive blocks.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty string. The recursion strictly processes shorter interiors, so it terminates for valid special strings.
Complexity: Recursive splitting and sorting can take O(n² log n) in a loose worst-case bound due to repeated substring creation; recursive space can be O(n²) cumulatively. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Produce the largest lexicographic arrangement of a special binary string.
Idea: Identify primitive balanced segments, recursively maximize each interior, and sort the resulting wrapped segments in descending order.
Technique and why it applies: count increases for '1' and decreases for '0'; a zero balance marks a complete primitive segment. Such segments can be reordered without breaking the special-string property, and descending order maximizes the concatenation.
Invariant: anchor marks the start of the next primitive segment and result contains completed transformed segments.
Edge cases: Empty string yields an empty result. The recursive calls operate only on interiors, which are shorter than the current segment.
Complexity: Scanning is linear per recursion level, while sorting primitive pieces adds sorting cost; worst-case time can be O(n² log n), with O(n) stored output plus recursion. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Count integers in [left,right] whose number of set bits is a prime number.
Idea: Convert each number to binary, count the '1' characters, and test that count against the set of possible primes.
Technique and why it applies: The maximum bit count is bounded by the integer width, so the small prime set covers every possible prime count under the problem's limits.
Invariant: The sum expression increments the result once for each number whose popcount is in primes.
Edge cases: Values with zero or one set bit are not counted because neither count is prime. The integer range is assumed nonnegative.
Complexity: For R-L+1 values and at most b bits each, time is O((R-L+1)b), and auxiliary space is O(b) for temporary binary strings. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return how many integers between L and R have a prime number of one-bits.
Idea: Count set bits by repeatedly clearing the lowest set bit, then check the count against a fixed prime set.
Technique and why it applies: n &= n-1 removes exactly one set bit each iteration. The result of bitCount is tested for membership in primes.
Invariant: result is the number of integers processed so far whose set-bit count is prime.
Edge cases: The prime set covers counts up to 19, sufficient for the usual bounded range. Zero has bit count zero and is not counted.
Complexity: For each number, bitCount costs O(number of set bits), bounded by the fixed integer width; overall O(R-L+1) under fixed-width constraints and O(1) extra space. The author O(log(R-L)) time label is incorrect for scanning every integer in the range.

Task and constraints: Partition s into as many parts as possible so each letter appears in at most one part.
Idea: Record first and last positions of each character, then merge overlapping character spans into partitions.
Technique and why it applies: Any partition containing a character must extend through that character's final occurrence. Overlapping spans are merged by expanding maxIndex; a gap closes the current partition and starts another.
Invariant: [start,maxIndex] is the active partition whose characters do not appear outside its boundary.
Edge cases: defaultdict is not imported in the shown code. It iterates spans in dictionary insertion order, which corresponds to first appearance order in Python; this is necessary for the merge logic.
Complexity: Building spans and merging them are O(n) time and O(u) space for distinct characters. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the lengths of maximum partitions where each character occurs in only one partition.
Idea: Record the last index of each character and extend the current partition endpoint while scanning.
Technique and why it applies: Every encountered character may occur later, so last is expanded to its final index. When the scan reaches last, all characters in the segment are complete and a partition can close.
Invariant: last is the farthest required endpoint for the current partition; first is its starting index.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty list. A character appearing late forces the active partition to extend through that occurrence.
Complexity: Building the last-index map and scanning the string take O(n) time and O(u) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Find the largest order of a plus sign made of ones in an N-by-N grid after specified mines are set to zero.
Idea: Initialize each cell with its horizontal run length, then refine it using all four directional run lengths.
Technique and why it applies: For each row, left-to-right and right-to-left scans compute horizontal arm limits. Column scans similarly compute vertical limits; each cell's possible plus order is the minimum of its four directional lengths.
Invariant: dp[i][j] stores the smallest run length seen in the directions processed so far, which bounds the plus centered there.
Edge cases: A mine forces the directional run to zero. If the grid has no mines, the center's order is determined by its distance to the nearest boundary.
Complexity: Four full scans cost O(N²) time and the DP matrix uses O(N²) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Minimize swaps needed to seat every couple together in adjacent pairs.
Idea: Build a person-to-seat map, then scan couch pairs and swap in the current person's partner when missing.
Technique and why it applies: Partner IDs are adjacent pairs: odd x pairs with x-1 and even x with x+1. The location map is updated alongside the row swap so later partner lookups remain valid.
Invariant: Every couch already processed has its two partners seated together; loc maps each person to their current seat.
Edge cases: The row is mutated. The formula correctly handles zero-based person labels with odd/even parity, assuming the standard labels 0 through n-1.
Complexity: Building the location map and scanning couples take O(n) time and O(n) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum swaps needed to make each couple sit together.
Idea: Represent each couch as a graph vertex and each couple as an edge between the couches occupied by its members.
Technique and why it applies: Couples whose members sit together create self-loops and are skipped. Each nontrivial cycle of couch relationships requires one fewer swap than its number of vertices; the code counts those edges while traversing adjacency lists.
Invariant: The traversal removes reverse adjacency links as it walks a cycle, preventing the same couch edge from being processed again.
Edge cases: A couch with no adjacency entries is already correct. The code assumes each couple appears exactly twice and each couch has two seats.
Complexity: Graph construction and cycle traversal are O(n) time and O(n) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Determine whether every matrix diagonal from top-left to bottom-right contains equal values.
Idea: Keep the first row as expected diagonal values, then compare each next row's suffix against that expected sequence.
Technique and why it applies: A Toeplitz matrix has each value equal to its upper-left neighbor. The code removes the first row's final value and checks each subsequent row shifted one position to the left.
Invariant: expected is intended to hold the diagonal values expected at the next row's columns.
Edge cases: The code mutates matrix rows by popping elements, including the original first row. It assumes nonempty rectangular input. Because expected references matrix[0], the first pop changes the input data.
Complexity: Each matrix value is compared or removed once, so O(mn) time and O(n) auxiliary state, but the implementation mutates input rows. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Check whether a matrix is Toeplitz, meaning each diagonal from top-left to bottom-right is constant.
Idea: Compare every cell not in the first row or first column with its upper-left neighbor.
Technique and why it applies: All diagonal entries after the first are constrained by the immediately preceding cell on that diagonal. If any pair differs, the matrix cannot be Toeplitz.
Invariant: Every cell checked so far matches the cell one row and one column above it.
Edge cases: The first row and first column begin diagonals and need no comparison. Empty matrices return True because no cell violates the condition, though constraints usually require at least one row.
Complexity: Each cell is checked once, giving O(mn) time and O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether all top-left-to-bottom-right diagonals have constant values.
Idea: Use all() over every matrix cell, accepting boundary cells and checking the upper-left neighbor for all others.
Technique and why it applies: A cell must equal matrix[i-1][j-1] whenever both coordinates are positive. This local equality for all cells is sufficient to guarantee every diagonal is constant.
Invariant: The generator tests the defining equality for each interior diagonal cell.
Edge cases: Empty input makes all() return True. The method does not mutate the matrix.
Complexity: The generator visits every cell, so time is O(mn) and auxiliary space O(1), matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum number of chunks that can be independently sorted so concatenation yields the fully sorted array, allowing duplicates.
Idea: Sort a copy, map each value to its sorted positions, and scan the original from right to left to find boundaries.
Technique and why it applies: For each original value, the code pops one target sorted position from its value's position list. idx tracks the minimum target position required by the suffix; when the current index equals idx, a chunk boundary is counted.
Invariant: idx is the earliest sorted position that must remain in the current suffix chunk for all processed values.
Edge cases: Duplicate values are handled through lists of sorted positions. defaultdict is referenced but not imported. The sorted positions are popped from the end, which pairs duplicates with target positions in reverse order.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), building and consuming position lists is O(n), and storage is O(n). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Maximize the number of chunks that can each be sorted independently to sort the whole array.
Idea: Maintain a monotonic stack of maximum values for the chunks formed so far.
Technique and why it applies: Each stack entry represents the maximum value of a completed or candidate chunk. When a new number is smaller than the last chunk maximum, chunks must merge; popping continues until the current number can be appended with the maximum of the merged region.
Invariant: The stack is non-decreasing and stores the maximum value of each current chunk.
Edge cases: Duplicate values are allowed. An empty array returns zero because the stack remains empty.
Complexity: Each value is pushed once and popped at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum number of chunks that can be sorted individually to produce the sorted permutation 0 through n-1.
Idea: Scan the permutation while tracking the maximum value seen so far and close a chunk whenever that maximum equals the current index.
Technique and why it applies: If the maximum prefix value is i, all values in the prefix must be at most i. Since the prefix contains i+1 distinct permutation values, it must contain exactly 0 through i, so sorting it cannot affect later positions.
Invariant: currentmax is the maximum of arr[0:i+1], and count records completed chunks.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero. This criterion relies on arr being a permutation of 0..n-1; it is not valid for arbitrary values or duplicates.
Complexity: One pass gives O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.
